name: Hydrocephalus: obstructive versus communicating
presentation: A child with a large head and a bulging fontanelle whose eyes are forced downward, or an adult with a morning headache that wakes them, vomiting, blurred vision from swollen optic discs and double vision from a sixth nerve palsy, has hydrocephalus. If the CT shows dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth, the block is in the aqueduct; if all four ventricles are dilated, the block is outside them, at the basal cisterns or the arachnoid granulations, after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

deficits.sign: Headache worse in the morning and on lying, vomiting, drowsiness; coma with acute obstruction
Papilledema with enlarged blind spots and transient visual obscurations; late optic atrophy
Sixth nerve palsies from raised pressure; sunset eyes and Parinaud signs from third ventricular dilatation pressing on the tectum
Spastic, magnetic gait from stretching of the leg fibers around the dilated frontal horns
Urgency and incontinence from stretched periventricular frontal fibers

reasoning: Cerebrospinal fluid is secreted by the choroid plexus of the lateral, third and fourth ventricles, flows through the foramina of Monro, the third ventricle, the aqueduct and the fourth ventricle, leaves through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie into the subarachnoid space and is absorbed into the venous sinuses through the arachnoid granulations. Obstruction anywhere along the route dilates the ventricles upstream of the block, and the pattern of dilatation locates it: a block at one foramen of Monro traps one lateral ventricle; a block in the aqueduct, the narrowest part, dilates both lateral ventricles and the third but leaves the fourth normal; a block at the fourth ventricular outlets dilates all four; and failure of absorption at the granulations or obstruction of the basal cisterns by blood, pus or carcinomatosis, called communicating hydrocephalus because the ventricles still communicate with the subarachnoid space, dilates all four together with the cisterns. The distinction matters because a lumbar puncture is dangerous in obstructive hydrocephalus, where the lumbar sac is not in communication with the ventricles and drainage can precipitate herniation, but is diagnostic and sometimes therapeutic in communicating hydrocephalus. The signs are those of raised intracranial pressure, bilateral and without an ipsilateral or contralateral pattern: papilledema from transmission of pressure along the optic nerve sheaths, sixth nerve palsies from stretching of the long abducens nerves, and, when the third ventricle balloons back over the tectum, the up-gaze palsy of the dorsal midbrain syndrome. The leg fibers of the corticospinal tract sweep around the frontal horns on their way to the internal capsule and are stretched first, giving the characteriztic gait and bladder disturbance.

imagingFindings.finding: Dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle (aqueduct stenosis or tectal tumor) or all four dilated with an outlet block; rounded frontal horns, periventricular low density from transependymal CSF flow, effaced sulci.
All four ventricles dilated with prominent basal cisterns; look for the cause: leptomeningeal enhancement, subarachnoid blood, previous meningitis.
Sagittal T2 and CISS show aqueduct stenosis, a tectal glioma, a colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro or a fourth ventricular tumor; absent aqueductal flow void.

commonCauses: Posterior fossa tumor or Chiari malformation
Colloid cyst of the third ventricle

mimics.name: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
mimics.howToDistinguish: Small or normal ventricles with papilledema

mimics.name: Cerebral atrophy (hydrocephalus ex vacuo)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Ventricles and sulci enlarged in proportion, no pressure signs

mimics.name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
mimics.howToDistinguish: Chronic triad in the elderly with normal opening pressure

management: Urgent CT in any patient with headache, vomiting and papilledema; do not perform a lumbar puncture in obstructive hydrocephalus
External ventricular drainage for acute obstruction; endoscopic third ventriculostomy for aqueduct stenosis; ventriculoperitoneal shunt for communicating forms
Treat the underlying tumor or cyst
